# Mei Lin — CV

## Education
- B.Eng., Computer Science, Tsinghua University, 2023–2027 (expected). GPA 3.86/4.0, rank 9/180.

## Research experience
- **Undergraduate researcher, Pervasive HCI Group, Tsinghua** (Sep 2025 – present), advised by Prof. Li Wei.
  Ran a 14-participant interview and diary study with blind screen-reader users on how they verify LLM answers;
  designed "SourceSpeak", a screen-reader plug-in that reads provenance cues aloud. In a within-subjects study
  (n = 12), participants caught 2.3x more incorrect answers with the plug-in. Paper under review at a major
  HCI conference (first author).
- **Research intern, Microsoft Research Asia, Beijing** (Jun – Aug 2026), mentor: Dr. Zhang Hua.
  Conversational-agent study with 20 older adults (65–82) and their adult children; found that error repair
  initiated by a family member doubled continued use over four weeks. Short paper accepted at a workshop.
- **Course project, Human-Centered AI (Spring 2026):** a constraint-based design tool that flags
  inaccessible colour contrast and focus order in Figma prototypes; used by 3 student teams.

## Publications
- M. Lin, J. Zhou, L. Wei. "SourceSpeak: Non-Visual Provenance Cues for LLM Answers." Under review, 2026 (first author).
- M. Lin, H. Zhang. "Family-Mediated Error Repair with Conversational Agents for Older Adults." Workshop paper, 2026.

## Skills
- Mixed-methods research (interviews, diary studies, thematic analysis), prototyping (React, Figma, Swift),
  statistics in R; screen-reader testing (NVDA, VoiceOver); Mandarin (native), English (fluent).

## Awards
- Tsinghua Outstanding Undergraduate Research Award, 2026. Second place, Tsinghua Accessibility Hackathon, 2025.

## Service
- Volunteer, Beijing Blind Technology Center, 2024–present (screen-reader training for new users).

items.text:
# Research interests

Human-computer interaction at the intersection of accessibility and large language models:

1. Screen-reader users and LLM interfaces: how blind and low-vision users verify what a model says, and
   interface designs that expose provenance (where an answer came from) non-visually.
2. Older adults and conversational agents in Chinese households: trust, repair after errors, and family
   mediation of technology use.
3. Mixed-methods evaluation: interview studies and diary studies combined with instrumented prototypes.

Secondary: design tools that let non-programmers specify accessible UI constraints; participatory design.

items.text:
# Statement of purpose — rough draft

I study how people who cannot see a screen can still tell when an AI is wrong. In my diary study with 14
blind screen-reader users, the most common strategy for checking an LLM answer was asking a sighted friend,
which is exactly the dependence these tools were supposed to remove. SourceSpeak, the plug-in I built in
response, reads provenance cues aloud; in a within-subjects study participants caught 2.3 times more incorrect
answers. That result is the core of my first-author submission.

At Microsoft Research Asia I looked at a different population with a related problem: older adults using
conversational agents. When a family member initiated the repair after an agent error, continued use over four
weeks doubled. Trust is repaired socially, not just technically.

In a PhD I want to design and evaluate interfaces that make AI provenance and errors legible to people who are
usually left out of the design process, using mixed methods and working prototypes.
